n: Jeremiah’s temple sermon (19:14-15) reaches Pashur, a priest who was also the chief officer responsible for order in the temple.

f.g: A different man from the Pashur son of Malchiah in 21:1. Immer was a priestly family.
Chief overseer—something like head of temple security.

n: Pashur has Jeremiah beaten and locked overnight in the stocks at a temple gate, where he would be exposed to public shame.

f.g: A wooden frame that held the feet (and perhaps hands and neck) in a painful, cramped position.
An upper gate on the north side of the temple area, facing Benjamin’s territory.

n: Released the next morning, Jeremiah is not intimidated. He gives Pashur a new name: “Magor-missabib.”

f.g: Hebrew “terror on every side,” a phrase Jeremiah uses often.

n: Pashur’s new name will describe his life: he will be a terror to himself and his friends as he watches them fall. Babylon is now named outright as the instrument of judgment.

f.g: Nebuchadnezzar II, who ruled about 605–562 BC.

n: All the city’s wealth—its produce, treasures, and royal riches—will be plundered and hauled to Babylon.

f.w: all the treasures of the kings of Judah

n: Pashur himself will go into exile and die in Babylon, along with friends to whom he had preached false comfort. He was not just a priest but a false prophet.
Now Jeremiah pours out his heart. He feels God overpowered him into this calling and left him a laughingstock. His honesty with God is part of what makes him so relatable.

f.g: Hebrew pittitani—“you enticed/persuaded me.” Jeremiah feels he was talked into a calling he couldn’t foresee.

n: Every time he speaks, his message is “Violence and destruction!”—and in return he gets only insults all day long.
He tried to quit—but God’s word burned inside him like fire trapped in his bones. He was worn out trying to hold it in and couldn’t. A powerful picture of a testimony that won’t stay silent.

f.w: a burning fire shut up in my bones

n: He hears whispering everywhere. Even his closest friends watch for him to slip, hoping to trap him and get revenge.

f.g: Hebrew magor missabib—the same phrase he used to rename Pashur, now turned against him by mockers.

n: Yet faith rises: the Lord is with him like a mighty warrior. His persecutors will stumble and be ashamed forever.
He commits his case to the Lord, who tests the righteous and sees into the deepest self.

f.g: Kidneys—in Hebrew thought, the seat of inner feelings and motives.

n: A sudden burst of praise: sing to the Lord, who rescues the poor from the wicked.

f.g: The needy and powerless—here Jeremiah counts himself among them.

n: Then just as suddenly he plunges into despair and curses the day he was born. These swings between praise and anguish show the real emotional cost of his mission.

f.w: Cursed be the day wherein I was born

n: He even curses the messenger who brought his father the happy news of his birth—a poetic way of wishing he had never existed.
May that messenger be like the cities God overthrew without pity (Sodom and Gomorrah), hearing alarms of war morning and noon.

f.w: the cities which the LORD overthrew

f.g: Did not relent or change his mind.

n: Because he wasn’t killed before birth—his mother’s womb could have been his grave. This is the language of deep grief, not a literal wish carried out.

Why was I born only to see trouble and sorrow and end my days in shame? The chapter ends unresolved, yet Jeremiah never stops serving. Even Joseph Smith in Liberty Jail would cry “O God, where art thou?”
